extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety managers, State Plan administrators, and public commenters on OSHA's heat standard NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and procedural requirements from OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Standard (NPRM) describing employer obligations (HIIPP, monitoring, acclimatization, emergency response, recordkeeping, signage, communications, and related provisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest break requirements at heat triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide a rest break if needed to prevent overheating at or above the initial heat trigger, and a rest break of at least 15 minutes every two hours at or above the high heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites scientific evidence that rest breaks, particularly combined with water and shade, reduce risk of heat-related fatalities and HRI and therefore requires rest breaks in the proposed standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical surveillance (ANSI/ASSP vs OSHA)
rubrics_metrics.description: ANSI/ASSP indicates a medical surveillance program (comprehensive work and medical history, comprehensive physical exam, assessment of personal risk factors, and ability to wear PPE) should be established; the OSHA proposed standard does not require medical surveillance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explains a medical surveillance requirement would be impractical and costly given the broad scope of the proposed standard and cites industry comments noting logistical difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and immediate care for employees with heat illness signs/symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must ensure an employee exhibiting signs or symptoms of heat illness is monitored, not left alone, and not sent home without being offered on-site first aid and, if necessary, emergency medical services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANSI/ASSP further requires a supervisor or team member trained in first aid and certified in CPR and AED when a medical professional is not available; OSHA's proposal does not require CPR/AED certification but requires monitoring and on-site first aid/EMS as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling personal protective equipment (PPE) use and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's proposed standard specifies engineering and administrative controls but does not require cooling PPE; employers who choose to provide cooling PPE must ensure the cooling properties of the PPE are maintained at all times during use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes cooling PPE (e.g., cooling vests) can become hazardous as cooling properties dissipate, so if provided employers must maintain their cooling function (see Section VII.E., Paragraph (e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping of indoor work area measurements and retention period
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must maintain written or electronic records of indoor work area measurements and retain those records for 6 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA considers this specificity (6-month retention) to increase clarity for employers compared to the ANSI/ASSP approach that requires written inventory only as long as the hazard exists or as required by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified person vs heat safety coordinator requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The ANSI/ASSP standard requires a 'qualified person' with recognized credentials or extensive knowledge to assist in program development; OSHA's proposed standard does not require a qualified person but requires designation of one or more heat safety coordinators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA believes requiring a qualified person would be infeasible for the wide scope of covered employers and instead requires heat safety coordinators who are trained and responsible for ensuring compliance with the employer's HIIPP; OSHA will provide compliance assistance materials (e.g., model HIIPP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard alerts when high heat trigger met
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's proposed standard contains a hazard alert provision requiring employers to notify employees that the high heat trigger has been met or exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA believes this notification is important to protect workers from heat hazards (see Section VII.F., Paragraph (f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning signs at indoor areas exceeding 120 °F
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must place a legible, visible, and understandable warning sign at indoor work areas with ambient temperatures that regularly exceed 120 °F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement appears in proposed §1910.148(f)(5) and is intended to alert workers to extreme indoor ambient temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NIOSH Publication No. 2016-106 (RAL/REL) as optional triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposes to incorporate by reference NIOSH Pub. 2016-106 and to propose the NIOSH Recommended Alert Limit (RAL) as an option for the initial heat trigger and the NIOSH Recommended Exposure Limit (REL) as an option for the high heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH Pub. 2016-106 is made available publicly (links provided) and is included in the rulemaking docket; the inclusion gives employers an established option for numeric heat triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP content requirements (§1910.148(c)(1)-(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must develop and implement a Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Plan (HIIPP) that includes a list of covered activities, the policies and procedures necessary to comply with the proposed standard, the heat metric the employer will use to comply with paragraph (d), and policies/procedures related to the use of vapor-impermeable clothing, if applicable. For employers with more than 10 employees, the HIIPP must be in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are collection-of-information elements specified in the ICR and are intended to ensure employers have documented plans tailored to their covered activities and chosen heat metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of heat safety coordinators (§1910.148(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must designate one or more heat safety coordinators to implement and monitor the HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat safety coordinators are the employer-level designees responsible for ensuring plan implementation and monitoring; training of these coordinators is required under the proposed standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee participation and HIIPP review (§1910.148(c)(6)-(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must seek the input and involvement of non-managerial employees in developing and implementing the HIIPP, and must review and evaluate the effectiveness of the HIIPP at least annually and whenever a heat-related illness or injury occurs that results in days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soliciting non-managerial input and periodic/incident-triggered reviews is intended to keep the HIIPP effective and responsive to workplace realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP availability and language access (§1910.148(c)(8)-(9))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must make the HIIPP readily available at the work site in a language each employee, supervisor, and heat safety coordinator understands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility of the plan (location and language) is required so that covered personnel can use and follow plan provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoor work area identification and monitoring plans (§1910.148(d)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: At indoor worksites, employers must identify each work area where employees are reasonably expected to be exposed at or above the initial heat trigger and develop a monitoring plan for each such area that includes measuring heat index or wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must evaluate and update monitoring plans whenever there is a change in production, processes, equipment, controls, or a substantial increase in outdoor temperature that could increase indoor heat exposure, and must seek input from non-managerial employees when identifying areas and developing/updating plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization protocol for new and returning employees (§1910.148(e)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded, employers must implement an acclimatization protocol for each new employee and each returning employee (away >14 days) during their first week on the job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may choose either a plan that incorporates the control measures required at the high heat trigger or a gradual acclimatization plan that slowly increases exposure each day; requirement does not apply if the employee consistently worked under same/similar conditions in past 14 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective two-way communication requirement (§1910.148(e)(9))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded, employers must maintain a means of effective, two-way communication with employees and regularly communicate with employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular communication is required to ensure employees can report issues, receive instructions, and be informed of conditions and protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-shift or high-trigger employee notifications (§1910.148(f)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the work shift or upon determining the high heat trigger is met/exceeded, employers must notify employees of the importance of drinking plenty of water, employees' right to take rest breaks if needed and required rest breaks, how to seek help and procedures to take in a heat emergency, and, for mobile work sites, the location of break area(s) and drinking water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notification ensures employees know hydration, rest, emergency procedures, and logistics (e.g., break area locations) before or during high-heat conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat emergency response plan content (§1910.148(g)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must develop and implement a heat emergency response plan as part of the HIIPP that includes emergency phone numbers, how employees can contact a supervisor and emergency medical services, designated individual(s) to ensure procedures are invoked, how to transport employees to a place reachable by EMS, clear directions to the work site, and procedures for responding to an employee experiencing signs and symptoms of heat-related illness or a heat emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive emergency planning facilitates prompt and coordinated responses to heat emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate required actions for employees in heat emergency (§1910.148(g)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employee is experiencing signs and symptoms of a heat emergency, the employer must take immediate actions to reduce the employee's body temperature, immediately contact emergency medical services, relieve them from duty, monitor them, ensure they are not left alone, and offer on-site first aid and medical services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These immediate response steps are mandatory to protect afflicted employees and to facilitate emergency care.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) comment topics
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA solicits public comments on the collection-of-information requirements and estimated burden hours, including whether the collections are necessary, accuracy of burden estimates, the quality/utility/clarity of the information collected, and ways to minimize the compliance burden (e.g., automation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should be limited to the ICR topics and may be submitted to OMB and the rulemaking docket; OSHA warns that comments are public records and to avoid submitting personal information.
